summary: Suggests a mechanism by which a user process can attach itself to the local SNMP agent on a host to implement portions of the MIB. The mechanism is local to the host. It was Experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A helper program can tell the main reporter on a computer, "I will answer questions about this part."

questions: how does smux register a mib subtree
subtitle: How helper programs on a host plug their own pieces of the MIB into the local SNMP agent.

tldr.problem: An SNMP agent run as a user process can easily read kernel variables, but it has trouble getting information from other user processes, such as routing protocol programs.
tldr.mechanism: SMUX lets a user process, called a SMUX peer, open a TCP connection to the local SNMP agent, register a MIB subtree, and then answer the agent's get, get-next and set requests for that subtree.
tldr.outcome: The memo was an Experimental protocol and its status is now Historic. It is local to a single host.

today: RFC 1227 was published as an Experimental protocol in May 1991, and its status is now Historic. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SMUX Exists
sections.content:
On a typical system, an agent that speaks SNMP is a user process that reads kernel variables to provide the Internet-standard MIB. That works while everything it needs sits in the kernel or in files. It gets awkward when other user processes, such as routing protocols, hold the information.

The SNMP multiplexing (SMUX) protocol is the fix. A user process, called a SMUX peer, starts an association with the local SNMP agent, registers itself, and later handles management operations for the objects in its MIB module. Taken to the limit, the agent only needs to know the SNMP group, and everything else can come from peers. The RFC says this suits a manufacturer that wants to give SNMP access to its operating system in binary form.
sections.plainLanguage: The main reporter cannot see inside every helper program. So the helpers sign up and answer the questions about their own topics.

sections.title: Request-Response and Cache-Ahead
sections.content:
The RFC describes two ways to join a MIB module to the agent. In the request-response model the agent passes each SNMP request to the peer that exported the module, and passes the peer's answer back to the management station. It is agent-driven, because the agent starts every exchange after registration.

In the cache-ahead model the peer periodically sends the agent its whole subtree. The agent answers retrievals itself, while set requests go straight to the peer. It is peer-driven.

SMUX itself is request-response only. A peer may use cache-ahead with other processes behind it, in which case it acts as a "firewall" for them. Each peer may define its own cache-ahead protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Either the reporter asks the helper every time, or the helper keeps handing the reporter an updated list. SMUX uses the asking way.

sections.title: How the Protocol Runs
sections.content:
The agent listens for incoming connections. After connecting, the peer sends an OpenPDU. If the agent declines, it sends a close PDU and closes the connection. If it accepts, it sends no response.

For each subtree it wants to register or unregister, the peer sends a RReqPDU, and the agent answers with a matching RRspPDU, in the same order as the requests. A peer that wants to raise a trap sends an SNMP Trap-PDU, which the agent passes on to the management stations it is configured to send traps to.

When the agent gets a GetRequest, GetNextRequest or SetRequest that touches a registered subtree, it sends the peer an equivalent PDU holding only the variables in that subtree. The peer does the operation and replies with a GetResponse-PDU, and the agent relays the combined result. Either side ends the association by sending a ClosePDU, closing the connection and releasing all registrations for it.

The PDUs are written in ASN.1 and encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules. Over TCP the agent listens on port 199, and no extra framing is needed because BER objects delimit themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper says hello, says which topics it covers, and then answers questions the reporter forwards. When either one is done, they say goodbye.

sections.title: Priorities, Sets and Get-Next
sections.content:
Each registration has an integer priority from 0 to (2^31)-1, and a lower value means a higher priority. Several peers can register the same subtree, but only at different priorities. If a priority is taken, the agent increments it until it finds a free one. The special value -1 asks for the highest available priority. The peer with the highest priority is the only one consulted for that subtree. The agent must also enforce a "subtree mounting effect": if one peer registered sysDescr and another later registers system, requests for sysDescr go to the second peer. An agent should refuse registrations above, at or below the SNMP and SMUX subtrees.

Set operations use a simple two-phase commit. The agent sends each participating peer a SetRequest with only its variables. Each peer accepts or refuses without doing the work, replying with error-status noError(0) or a non-zero error. If any peer refuses, the agent sends every peer an SOutPDU with rollback. If all accept, it sends commit. Peers do not answer the SOutPDU.

For get-next, each peer acts as though it holds the entire MIB. The agent must check that each returned variable is still inside the subtree that caused the request, and for any that is not, ask the peer for the next registered subtree.
sections.plainLanguage: If two helpers want the same topic, the one with the lower number wins. For changes, the reporter first asks everyone "can you do this?" and only then says "go" or "cancel."

sections.title: The SMUX MIB
sections.content:
The memo also defines a MIB for SMUX itself, which the local agent must implement. It sits under smux, which is { unix 4 }, itself under enterprises 4. It has two tables.

The smuxPeerTable has one entry per peer, with an index, the peer's identity, a description of up to 255 characters, and a status of valid(1), invalid(2) or connecting(3). The smuxTreeTable is indexed by subtree and priority and lists the registered subtrees, the peer's index and a status of valid(1) or invalid(2). Setting a status to invalid(2) invalidates the entry, and whether the agent then removes the row is implementation specific.
sections.plainLanguage: The reporter keeps two lists: who the helpers are, and which topic each one covers.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content: The OpenPDU carries a version (only version-1(0)), the peer's identity, a description and a password. A zero-length password means no authentication. The RFC calls this "simple authentication" and nothing more is defined. The Security Considerations section states only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper can show a password when it says hello, but the memo does not say much more about keeping things safe.

messages.label: OpenPDU
messages.note: Sent after the TCP connection is up.

messages.label: Equivalent request
messages.note: Only variables in the registered subtree.

viz.caption: SMUX PDU TYPES AND THEIR APPLICATION TAGS

items.label: SimpleOpen
items.desc: Opens the association: version, identity, description and password.

items.label: ClosePDU
items.desc: Ends the association, with a reason code from 0 (goingDown) to 5 (authenticationFailure).

items.label: RReqPDU
items.desc: Register or delete a subtree: delete(0), readOnly(1), readWrite(2).

items.label: RRspPDU
items.desc: Registration answer: failure(-1) or the priority granted.
